title: Introduction to Life Assurance: Concepts and Terminology

blocks.h: On completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

items.h: Explain the terminological distinction between 'life assurance' and 'life insurance' and describe when each term is appropriately used.
State the four classes of life insurance business as defined by NIIRA 2025 and describe the scope of each.
Identify and define the parties to a life assurance contract: proposer, life assured, policyholder, beneficiary, nominee, and annuitant.
Define the key monetary terms of a life policy: sum assured, premium, policy term, maturity value, and face amount.
Explain the different premium payment modes and describe the operation of the grace period and the 'no premium, no cover' rule.
Distinguish between the death benefit, maturity benefit, and survival benefits of a life assurance policy.
Define and calculate surrender value and paid-up value, and explain the circumstances in which each arises.
Explain the mechanics of a policy loan and the lien arrangement, and describe the conditions under which each is available.
Distinguish between participating (with-profit) and non-participating (without-profit) policies and explain the nature of reversionary, terminal, and interim bonuses.
Summarise NIIRA 2025's requirements for life policy disclosure, the cooling-off right, and mandatory beneficiary protections.

blocks.text: 5.1  Introduction: The Vocabulary of Life Assurance

blocks.h: Every profession has a vocabulary. The vocabulary of life assurance is not merely technical jargon — it is the precise language through which obligations are created, benefits are defined, and rights are exercised. The term 'sum assured' is not a synonym for 'payment'; it is a specific legal and contractual concept with a defined relationship to the premium, to the actuarial basis of the policy, and to the claims settlement process. The distinction between 'proposer' and 'life assured' is not pedantic; it determines who has legal standing to alter, surrender, or assign the policy. The difference between a 'reversionary bonus' and a 'terminal bonus' has direct financial consequences for a policyholder who surrenders a participating policy before maturity.

This chapter provides the vocabulary for everything that follows in Part Two and beyond. It proceeds in a deliberate sequence: from the overarching question of what we call this type of insurance (Section 5.2), through the statutory classification of life insurance classes in Nigeria (Section 5.3), to the parties who stand in relation to a life assurance contract (Section 5.4), and then through each of the key monetary and operational concepts that define how a life policy works from inception to claim. The chapter concludes with NIIRA 2025's consumer disclosure requirements — the regulatory framework within which every life policy sold in Nigeria from August 2025 forward must be presented to prospective policyholders.

Readers who come to this chapter from a background in general insurance — property, motor, marine — will find that several familiar concepts operate differently, or not at all, in the life context. The indemnity principle has limited application. Subrogation is absent. The premium payment obligation is more complex. The claims settlement process involves a different category of documentation. These differences are not merely procedural — they reflect the fundamentally different nature of life assurance as a product: long-term, personal, partially savings-based, and actuarially driven in a way that non-life insurance is not.

blocks.text: 5.2  'Life Assurance' and 'Life Insurance': The Terminological Debate

blocks.h: In the classical tradition of English and Nigerian insurance law and practice, the terms 'assurance' and 'insurance' are not interchangeable. The distinction reflects the fundamental difference between a certainty and a contingency.

items.h: Insurance refers to cover against an event that may or may not occur during the policy period. Motor insurance covers the contingency of an accident; fire insurance covers the contingency of a fire. If neither event occurs, the insurer has no obligation to pay.

Assurance refers to cover against an event that will certainly occur — the only uncertainty is when. Death is certain; the only question is the timing. A whole life policy is therefore properly described as 'life assurance,' because the insurer's obligation to pay is not contingent on an uncertain event but is assured — it will pay, upon the death of the life assured, regardless of when that death occurs.

blocks.h: This distinction, while conceptually precise, is not universally observed in commercial practice. Term assurance — which pays only if the life assured dies within a defined period and pays nothing if he survives — is technically 'life insurance' (because the payment is contingent, not assured) rather than 'life assurance' (because the insurer may never need to pay at all). Yet it is universally described as 'assurance' in Nigerian industry usage.<sup>[15]</sup>

NIIRA 2025 itself does not make the assurance-insurance terminological distinction explicitly. The Act uses the phrase 'life insurance' as the umbrella category, with 'individual life assurance' as one of the four designated sub-classes. Nigerian insurance companies use both terms commercially, often within the same organisation: a company may call itself 'Assurance' in its corporate name (Leadway Assurance, African Alliance Insurance, ARM Life Assurance) and yet issue 'insurance' policies in its marketing materials.<sup>[1]</sup>

A long-term insurance contract under which the insurer undertakes to pay a specified sum (the sum assured) on the death of the life assured, or on the occurrence of another specified life event (survival to maturity, diagnosis of a critical illness, attainment of an annuity commencement age). The term 'assurance' is used because the event that triggers payment — death — is certain; only its timing is uncertain. In Nigerian statutory usage under NIIRA 2025, the umbrella term is 'life insurance,' encompassing individual life assurance, group life assurance, annuity, and health insurance business.

Note: In practice, the terms 'life assurance' and 'life insurance' are used interchangeably in Nigerian commercial and regulatory discourse. This work uses 'life assurance' for individual and group long-term contracts and 'life insurance' as the statutory umbrella, consistent with NIIRA 2025 usage.

Despite its inconsistent commercial application, the assurance-insurance distinction retains analytical importance for three reasons. First, it illuminates the actuarial difference between products: whole life assurance carries a certainty of payment that must be fully funded by premiums; term insurance carries only a conditional payment obligation, making it structurally cheaper to price. Understanding why a term policy costs far less than a whole life policy for the same sum assured requires understanding this distinction.

Second, the distinction clarifies the indemnity question. As discussed in Chapter 2, the strict indemnity principle applies to non-life insurance but not to life assurance. The reason is precisely the certainty of the life event: you cannot indemnify someone for the loss of their own life (it cannot be quantified) nor for the loss of another's (the financial loss is too diffuse and personal to measure). Life assurance therefore pays a pre-agreed sum assured — not an indemnity for a measured loss.

Third, the distinction alerts practitioners to the different regulatory classification of 'long-term' versus 'short-term' insurance business. The separation of life and non-life funds — required under NIIRA 2025 and maintained by the statutory separation of life insurance licences — reflects this structural difference. A policy that straddles the boundary (a term policy with an investment component, for example) requires careful classification to ensure it is licensed, rated, and reported under the correct regulatory category.

blocks.text: 5.3  The Four Classes of Life Insurance Business Under NIIRA 2025

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 provides formal statutory classification of life insurance business into four distinct classes. This classification is the basis on which NAICOM issues life insurance licences, and it determines the regulatory, actuarial, and operational requirements that apply to each type of business:<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup>

rows: Cover for individual lives under personal policies. The proposer is typically the same person as the life assured, though third-party life policies (e.g. keyman) are included. Policies are personal contracts.
Term assurance; whole life; endowment; anticipated endowment (money-back); investment-linked life; critical illness; mortgage protection
Cover for a defined group of lives, typically employees of a common employer. A master policy is issued to the employer (the policyholder); individual employees receive certificates of participation.
Employer-sponsored death-in-service cover; Group Term Assurance; Group Credit Life; Directors and Officers death benefit schemes

Contracts providing a periodic income stream, typically for life or for a defined period, in exchange for a single premium or accumulated fund. Includes the Retirement Life Annuity (RLA) mandated by the Pension Reform Act 2014.
Immediate annuities; deferred annuities; Retirement Life Annuities (RLA); joint-life annuities; annuities certain

Contracts covering the financial consequences of illness, injury, or hospitalisation. Includes both indemnity-based medical expense cover and fixed-benefit products such as hospital cash and critical illness insurance.
Comprehensive medical insurance; hospital cash plans; critical illness insurance; income protection insurance; disability income insurance

blocks.h: Sources: Pavestones Legal, 'NIIRA 2025 — Navigating Compliance,' 2025; <sup>[1]</sup> Afriwise, 'NIIRA 2025 Regulatory Update,' 2025.<sup>[2]</sup>

This four-class architecture has important implications for practitioners. A life insurer must hold a licence specifically authorising each class of business it writes. A life insurer licensed for 'individual life assurance' is not automatically authorised to write group schemes (class 2) or annuities (class 3). NAICOM's product approval process operates within these class boundaries: a product that blends individual life assurance with an annuity phase (such as an endowment that converts to an annuity at maturity) requires regulatory analysis to determine whether it falls within one class or constitutes a combined product requiring dual authorisation.

blocks.title: Regulatory Spotlight — NIIRA 2025 — Life Insurance Licence Classes and Separation of Business

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025's classification of life insurance business has direct operational consequences:

items.h: A new insurer entering the market must specify in its application which of the four life classes it intends to write, and must satisfy NAICOM's capital, actuarial, and governance requirements for each class applied for.

An insurer licensed for annuity business carries specific additional obligations: annuity policies are specifically excluded from the Standalone Insurtech licensing category, meaning that no Insurtech may write annuity products without a full conventional life licence.

Health insurance written by a NAICOM-licensed life insurer must comply with both NAICOM requirements and, where the product involves active care management, with the National Health Insurance Authority Act 2022. The dual-regulation obligation is clearest for products that reimburse actual medical expenses.

Group life assurance written under the Pension Reform Act 2014 mandate must meet the minimum sum assured of three times annual total emolument per employee. Penalties for employer non-compliance are ₦250,000 per uninsured employee under NIIRA 2025.

blocks.h: Practitioners should confirm at the proposal stage whether the envisaged product falls within the insurer's licensed classes. An insurer that quotes or underwrites a product outside its licensed classes is in regulatory breach, and the policy may be unenforceable.<sup>[10]</sup>

blocks.text: 5.4  Parties to a Life Assurance Contract

blocks.h: A life assurance policy may involve more individuals than any other financial contract of comparable simplicity. Understanding who stands in what legal relationship to the policy is essential for every aspect of its administration — from the initial proposal to the payment of a claim.

The proposer is the person who applies for the insurance — who completes the proposal form, offers the premium, and enters into the contract with the insurer. In a policy taken out by an individual on their own life, the proposer and the life assured are the same person. In a keyman policy taken out by a company on the life of a key executive, the proposer is the company. In an employer's group life scheme, the proposer is the employer.

The person or entity that completes the proposal form and enters into the insurance contract with the insurer. The proposer bears the duty of utmost good faith at the proposal stage — it is the proposer who must make full and accurate disclosure of all material facts. The proposer is the insured for the purpose of the policy, regardless of whether the proposer is also the life assured.

Note: In Nigerian life assurance practice, 'proposer' and 'policyholder' are sometimes used interchangeably in policy documents, though strictly the proposer is the person at the application stage and the policyholder is the person who holds the policy after acceptance.

The life assured is the person on whose life the policy is taken out — the individual whose death, survival, or health event triggers the benefit payment. In an own-life policy, the proposer and the life assured are the same person. In a third-party life policy, they are different. The life assured is not necessarily a party to the contract: an employee covered under a group life master policy has no contractual relationship with the insurer — the employer is the policyholder, and the employee is merely the life on which the risk is written.

This distinction has practical implications in claims processing. When the life assured dies and the proposer/policyholder is a different person (a surviving spouse, an employer, a bank as mortgagee), it is the policyholder who makes the claim, not the estate of the life assured. The life assured's will, letters of administration, and probate are relevant to determining who is beneficially entitled to the proceeds, but it is the policyholder's contractual right to make the claim.

The policyholder is the person who holds the policy after it has been issued — the owner of the contractual rights. In most retail life assurance, the proposer becomes the policyholder on acceptance. The policyholder has the right to alter the policy (subject to underwriting), to nominate or change the beneficiary, to assign the policy, to take a policy loan, to surrender the policy, and to make a claim.

The distinction between policyholder and life assured becomes commercially significant in the following scenarios: a parent who takes out an endowment policy on a child's life is the policyholder; the child is the life assured. A wife who takes out a life policy on her husband's life is the policyholder; the husband is the life assured. A lender who holds a life policy as mortgage security is the assignee (and effectively the temporary policyholder); the borrower is the life assured.

The beneficiary is the person (or entity) designated to receive the policy proceeds on the occurrence of the specified event — death, maturity, or critical illness. As discussed in Chapter 3, a beneficiary may be designated through a formal nomination (in which the policyholder names a person to receive the proceeds but does not transfer ownership) or through an assignment (in which the policyholder transfers ownership of the policy to the designated person).

In Nigerian life assurance practice, the nomination mechanism is by far the more common. A policyholder names their spouse, children, or other dependants as nominees. The nominee receives the proceeds as the policyholder's representative — but the proceeds form part of the policyholder's estate and may be subject to the claims of creditors unless the policy is written under trust or assigned irrevocably.

The person or entity designated by the policyholder to receive the policy proceeds on the occurrence of the specified event (typically death). A nominee under a nomination clause receives the proceeds as the policyholder's representative without the proceeds being legally separated from the estate. A beneficiary under a trust arrangement or an assignment receives the proceeds as beneficial or legal owner, outside the policyholder's estate. NIIRA 2025 requires insurers to maintain current beneficiary records and to provide accessible procedures for updating nominations.
See: Chapter 3 (Assignment and Nomination); NIIRA 2025, consumer protection provisions.

The annuitant is the person on whose life an annuity contract is written — the person in respect of whose survival or death the annuity payments continue or cease. In a life annuity contract, the insurer agrees to pay a specified periodic income for as long as the annuitant lives. The annuitant is typically the same person as the policyholder in a retail annuity; in a group annuity arrangement funded by a pension scheme, the annuitant is the retiring employee and the policyholder may be the scheme trustee.

The annuitant concept is particularly important in the context of Nigeria's Retirement Life Annuity (RLA) regime under the Pension Reform Act 2014. The retiree who purchases an RLA from a licensed life insurer using their accumulated Retirement Savings Account balance is both the annuitant (in whose life the income stream is vested) and the policyholder. The annuity income is paid to the annuitant for life; on death, any guaranteed period payments continue to the estate or named beneficiary.

blocks.text: 5.5  Key Monetary Terms: Sum Assured, Premium, Policy Term, and Maturity

blocks.h: The sum assured is the amount the insurer contractually undertakes to pay on the occurrence of the specified event — the core financial commitment of the life assurance policy. It is agreed between the parties at inception and stated in the policy schedule. For a term assurance, the sum assured is the death benefit payable if the life assured dies within the policy term. For a whole life policy, it is the benefit payable on death at any time while the policy is in force. For an endowment, it is payable on death during the policy term or on survival to the maturity date, whichever occurs first.

The sum assured is not the same as the sum insured in property insurance. The sum insured in property insurance represents a cap on the insurer's indemnity — it limits recovery to the actual loss up to the sum insured. The sum assured in life assurance is the guaranteed payment — it is paid in full on the occurrence of the specified event regardless of the 'actual' financial loss. A life assured with a ₦50 million sum assured and a ₦20 million annual income will, on death, pay ₦50 million to beneficiaries whether or not their actual financial need equals that figure.

The pre-agreed amount that an insurer contractually undertakes to pay on the occurrence of the specified insured event under a life assurance policy. It is stated in the policy schedule at inception and is not subject to measurement of actual financial loss. In participating (with-profit) policies, the sum assured is augmented by declared bonuses to produce the total benefit payable at claim.
Cf: Sum Insured (property insurance) — the ceiling on indemnity recovery, measured against actual financial loss. Sum Assured is a guarantee; Sum Insured is a cap.

The face amount is synonymous with the basic sum assured for most purposes. In the context of participating (with-profit) policies, the face amount is the initial guaranteed sum assured before the addition of bonuses. Practitioners use 'face amount' most commonly when emphasising the guaranteed baseline of a policy benefit as distinct from the enhanced amount payable at claim (sum assured plus accrued reversionary bonuses plus any terminal bonus).

The premium is the monetary consideration paid by the policyholder to the insurer in exchange for the assumption of the specified risk. In life assurance, the premium is typically calculated by the insurer's actuarial function based on the age of the life assured, the sum assured, the policy type, the policy term, the payment mode, underwriting adjustments for health or occupational risk, and an expense and profit loading.

The premium is not merely a price — it is a contractual obligation. The 'no premium, no cover' rule under NIIRA 2025 means that the insurer's obligations to the policyholder are conditional on premiums being paid when due. An unpaid premium does not automatically void the policy (a grace period applies under most policy conditions) but it suspends the insurer's obligations for the duration of non-payment and may, if the lapse rules apply, put the policy into a reduced or lapsed status.

blocks.title: Illustration — Premium Calculation — A Simplified Life Assurance Example

blocks.h: Consider the following scenario: Chukwuemeka, a 35-year-old male non-smoker in Lagos, applies for a 20-year term assurance with a sum assured of ₦10 million. The insurer's actuarial assumptions include:

items.h: Annual probability of death (qx) for a 35-year-old Nigerian male: approximately 0.0028 (EFU Life Table)
Expected average premium-paying years: 20
Investment return assumption for discounting: 9% per annum
Expense loading: 15% of premium
Profit loading: 5% of premium

blocks.h: The net annual premium (the actuarial cost of the risk before expenses) is calculated as the present value of the expected claim cost over 20 years, taking into account the probability of death in each year. For this risk profile, a net annual premium of approximately ₦21,000 to ₦28,000 might be indicated before expense and profit loadings. With a 20% combined loading, the gross annual premium would be approximately ₦25,200 to ₦33,600.

This illustrates a key feature of term assurance: it provides ₦10 million of protection for a premium that represents approximately 0.25% to 0.33% of the sum assured per year — making it the most affordable form of life cover per unit of protection. The actual market rate in Nigeria varies by insurer and underwriting profile: Leadway Assurance, for example, offers a pre-priced term plan at ₦10,000 per year for ₦1 million of cover — a rate accessible even to lower-income earners.
Source: Leadway Assurance, Term Life Plan, <sup>[5]</sup>; EFU Life Table (actuarial standard for Nigeria).
Life assurance premiums may be paid in a variety of modes, providing flexibility for different cash flow patterns:

items.h: Single premium: The entire premium for the policy is paid as one lump sum at inception. Common for investment-linked policies, immediate annuities, and credit life insurance. There is no future payment obligation and the policy remains in force indefinitely (for whole life) or until maturity (for endowments).
Regular premiums: Paid periodically throughout the policy term or a defined premium-paying period.
Annual: One payment per year. Generally the lowest total cost due to the time value of the premium instalments.
Semi-annual: Two payments per year, typically at a small loading above the annual rate.
Quarterly: Four payments per year, at a slightly higher loading.

Monthly: Twelve payments per year. The most accessible mode for salaried employees with regular income but no ability to commit to a large annual sum. Employers often deduct monthly premiums from payroll (salary deduction at source) in group and worksite schemes.

Limited payment: Premiums are paid for a defined period shorter than the policy term (e.g. a 25-year whole life policy with premiums payable for only 15 years). Higher annual premium, but no payment obligation in the later years of the policy. Appeals to policyholders who expect their income-earning years to be limited by retirement age.

blocks.title: Advisory — Modal Premium Loadings — Pricing and Advice Guidance

blocks.h: When a policyholder chooses a payment mode other than annual, the insurer applies a modal loading — an additional charge to compensate for the time value of money (premiums received quarterly are worth less, in aggregate, than the same amount received annually) and for the additional administrative cost of processing more frequent payments. Typical modal loadings used in Nigerian practice:

Advisers should present the total annual cost across modes transparently, ensuring clients understand that the convenience of monthly payment comes at a premium. Where a client has irregular income (agricultural workers, traders, informal sector workers), flexible premium products — including monthly-renewable term assurance — may be more appropriate than conventional regular-premium endowments.

The policy term is the period during which the insurance cover is in force. In term assurance, it is the specified period (5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 years) during which death cover is active; at the end of the term, if the life assured survives, the policy expires with no payment. In endowment assurance, it is the period at the end of which the maturity benefit is payable if the life assured survives. In whole life assurance, there is no fixed policy term — the policy is in force for the lifetime of the life assured.

The concept of entry age and maximum entry age defines who can apply for a given policy: most Nigerian life insurers accept new applications from lives aged 18 to 65, with the maximum age at maturity typically set at 70 (extendable to 75 for certain products). The policy term must therefore be consistent with both the entry age and the maximum maturity age.

Maturity is the date on which an endowment, money-back, or savings-type life assurance policy reaches the end of its specified term and the maturity benefit becomes payable to the surviving policyholder. The maturity benefit is the amount guaranteed at inception to be payable if the life assured survives to the end of the policy term — the sum assured, plus (in participating policies) all accrued reversionary bonuses and any terminal bonus declared at maturity.

Maturity is the defining aspiration of many Nigerian retail life policies. The money-back (anticipated endowment) policy, which dominates the Nigerian retail market, pays interim survival benefits during the policy term and a final maturity sum at the end — combining the investment appeal of a savings product with the protection of life cover. The maturity benefit is what salespeople most prominently illustrate when presenting these products, and it is the marketing anchor for the largest segment of the Nigerian retail life market.

The date on which a fixed-term life assurance policy reaches the end of its specified term and the maturity benefit becomes payable to the surviving policyholder. The maturity benefit is the sum assured plus, in participating policies, all declared reversionary bonuses and any terminal bonus. Maturity is the policyholder's 'success scenario' — the outcome where both protection and savings objectives are fulfilled.
Note: Whole life policies do not have a maturity date. Annuities do not mature — they pay an income for as long as specified. Term assurance expires at the end of the term without a maturity benefit.

blocks.text: 5.6  Premium Payment: Grace Period, Lapse, and Revival

blocks.h: The grace period is a defined period after a premium due date during which the policy remains in force despite the premium not having been paid. If the life assured dies during the grace period, most policies pay the full death benefit less the unpaid premium (and any outstanding policy loan). The purpose of the grace period is to protect the policyholder from an accidental lapse caused by a delayed payment — it provides a safety net for temporary cash flow difficulties without immediately voiding the cover.

Standard practice in Nigeria and internationally is a grace period of 30 days for annual, semi-annual, and quarterly premium modes, and 15 days for monthly premium modes. The grace period is stated explicitly in the policy conditions. An insurer that relies on the expiry of the grace period to deny a death claim must demonstrate that the premium was not received within the grace period and that the policy had, by its terms, lapsed before the date of death.

A defined period (typically 15–30 days depending on the premium mode) following the premium due date during which the policy remains in force despite the premium being unpaid. If the insured event occurs during the grace period, the benefit is payable less the outstanding premium. On expiry of the grace period without payment, the policy lapses.

Note: Section 60 of NIIRA 2025 makes payment of the premium a condition of cover. Cover during a grace period therefore rests on the terms of the policy itself; the Act, as reviewed, sets no statutory minimum grace period. Check the policy conditions and current NAICOM guidance.

A policy lapses when the premium is not paid within the grace period, causing the policy to cease to be in force. A lapsed policy provides no death cover; the insurer has no obligation to pay on death after the lapse date. The policy may acquire a paid-up value or a surrender value depending on the number of premiums paid before lapse — these mechanisms are discussed below.

Lapse is the single largest driver of value destruction in the Nigerian retail life assurance market. A policyholder who lapses a long-term savings policy in the early years of its life — before the surrender value has built to a meaningful level — may receive nothing back despite having paid premiums for two or three years. The combination of high lapse rates and low policy persistency contributes to poor investment returns for the insurance industry as a whole and erodes consumer trust. NAICOM's market conduct guidelines address lapse management as a policyholder welfare concern.

Most life policies include a provision allowing the policyholder to revive (reinstate) a lapsed policy within a specified period — typically two to five years from the date of lapse. Revival requires payment of all outstanding premiums (usually with interest), and the submission of fresh medical evidence of the life assured's continued good health. The insurer has discretion to decline revival if the life assured's health has deteriorated materially since inception.

Revival is an important customer retention tool. An insurer with an effective conservation and revival programme can recover lapsed policies that would otherwise result in a complete loss of the premium relationship. NIIRA 2025's consumer service framework encourages insurers to proactively contact policyholders before the grace period expires and to offer payment alternatives (premium reduction, extended term, paid-up conversion) rather than allowing a simple lapse.

blocks.title: Advisory — Lapse Management — An Operational Priority

blocks.h: Lapse rates in Nigerian life insurance are historically high, driven by premium affordability constraints, economic volatility, and inadequate policyholder servicing. A structured lapse management programme should include:

items.h: Automated pre-lapse alerts: SMS, email, and app push notifications sent 10, 5, and 2 days before the grace period expires.
Conservation calls: Trained conservation officers contact the policyholder before the grace period ends to understand the reason for non-payment and offer solutions.
Premium holiday provisions: Where the policy allows, offer a temporary suspension of premiums (funded by the policy's surrender value) during periods of financial difficulty.
Reduced paid-up conversion: Where the policyholder cannot resume premium payments, convert the policy to a paid-up policy at a reduced sum assured rather than allowing a full lapse.

Revival campaign: Periodically contact lapsed policyholders within the revival window with a clear offer of reinstatement, emphasising the value of the accrued tenure and the reduced cost of fresh cover given their now-older age.

blocks.h: Every policy that lapses in year 1 or 2 is a complete financial loss for both the policyholder (who recovers nothing) and ultimately for the insurer (which recovers only the early-year premiums against higher first-year costs). Persistency improvement — reducing the lapse rate — is one of the highest-return operational investments a Nigerian life insurer can make.

blocks.text: 5.7  Policy Benefits: Death Benefit, Maturity Benefit, and Survival Benefits

blocks.h: The death benefit is the sum payable by the insurer on the death of the life assured while the policy is in force. It is the primary protection benefit of any life assurance policy. For term assurance, the death benefit is the only benefit; no payment is made on survival. For whole life and endowment policies, the death benefit is payable at any time during the policy term. For participating policies, the death benefit is the sum assured plus all accrued reversionary bonuses and any interim or terminal bonus declared for the period to the date of death.<sup>[6]</sup>

The death benefit is paid to the policyholder's nominated beneficiary, the assignee (where the policy has been assigned), or the policyholder's estate in the absence of a valid nomination. It is a contractual payment, not an indemnity: the insurer is obligated to pay the stated amount regardless of the policyholder's actual financial need at the time of death.

Many Nigerian life assurance products — particularly the 'money-back' or anticipated endowment — include survival benefits: periodic payments made during the policy term to a surviving life assured. These are a distinctive feature of Indian-origin product designs that have been adopted enthusiastically in the Nigerian market.

A typical money-back policy might pay 20% of the sum assured at the end of the fifth policy year, another 20% at the end of the tenth year, and a further 20% at the end of the fifteenth year, with the remaining 40% plus bonuses payable at maturity (year 20). Throughout this period, the full sum assured is payable on death regardless of how many survival benefits have already been paid. This is the product feature that most distinguishes anticipated endowments from conventional savings accounts: the life cover is not reduced by the receipt of survival benefits.

The maturity benefit is the sum payable at the end of the policy term to a surviving policyholder. It represents the 'investment side' of the policy — the accumulated savings component. In participating policies, the maturity benefit is the basic sum assured plus all accrued reversionary bonuses plus any terminal bonus declared by the insurer at maturity. In non-participating products, the maturity benefit is simply the guaranteed sum assured stated at inception.

Practitioners must be careful in the presentation of maturity benefits not to overstate the investment return. A participating policy's maturity benefit includes non-guaranteed elements (reversionary bonuses that have been declared and vested, plus a discretionary terminal bonus). The non-guaranteed nature of the terminal bonus must be disclosed clearly under NIIRA 2025's consumer protection standards. Projections of maturity benefits must use NAICOM-prescribed illustration rates where specified, or must be clearly labelled as illustrative and not guaranteed.

The surrender value is the amount the insurer pays to the policyholder who voluntarily terminates a policy before its maturity date or the death of the life assured. It is available on endowment and whole life policies after a minimum number of premiums have been paid (typically three years of annual premiums) but is not available on term assurance (which has no savings element) or in the very early years of savings policies (when the accumulated reserve has not yet exceeded the initial expenses).

The surrender value is invariably less than the total premiums paid in the early years of a policy — sometimes dramatically so. This is because the insurer's first-year expenses (commission, underwriting, policy issue costs) are amortised over the full expected policy term; when the policyholder surrenders early, the insurer recovers those expenses from the surrender value, leaving the policyholder with a fraction of what they paid. This 'front-loading' of costs is the reason why surrender values are low in the first three to five policy years and the reason why advisers should only recommend surrender as a last resort.
Two measures of surrender value are relevant in practice:<sup>[11]</sup>

items.h: Guaranteed Surrender Value (GSV): The minimum surrender value guaranteed in the policy document, typically calculated as a percentage of total premiums paid (less the cost of the term protection element). The GSV factor increases with policy duration.

Special Surrender Value (SSV): Usually higher than the GSV, the SSV reflects the actual asset share of the policy — the proportionate share of the insurer's actual investment returns allocated to the policy. For participating policies, the SSV also includes the surrender value of vested reversionary bonuses.

blocks.h: In the Nigerian market, the SSV is typically the operative surrender value after the third policy year. However, many policyholders are unaware that the SSV is higher than the GSV, and may receive less than they are entitled to if they accept the insurer's initial surrender quotation without questioning it. NIIRA 2025's consumer protection provisions require insurers to provide accurate and complete surrender value quotations upon request, and NAICOM has signalled that deliberately low surrender value quotations constitute a form of market conduct malpractice.

The amount payable by an insurer to a policyholder who voluntarily terminates a long-term life assurance policy before its maturity date. Available only after a minimum number of premiums have been paid. In Nigerian practice, the operative measure is typically the Special Surrender Value (SSV), which is higher than the guaranteed minimum (GSV). Surrender is financially disadvantageous in the early policy years due to the front-loading of acquisition costs.
Formula (GSV): GSV = Total Premiums Paid × GSV Factor (as per policy table). Formula (SSV): SSV = (Paid-up Value × SSV Factor) + Surrender Value of Bonuses.

The paid-up value is the reduced sum assured at which a policy continues in force without further premium payments, following the cessation of premium payment after the minimum number of premiums has been paid. Instead of surrendering the policy for cash, the policyholder asks the insurer to 'make the policy paid-up' — converting it to a smaller policy that remains in force until death or maturity without any further premium obligation.

The paid-up value is calculated as the proportion of the original sum assured represented by the number of premiums actually paid out of the total number due. If a 20-year endowment with a sum assured of ₦2 million has premiums paid for 10 years, the paid-up value is approximately ₦1 million (10 years paid ÷ 20 years total × ₦2 million sum assured = ₦1 million, subject to the exact paid-up value table in the policy). In a participating policy, the accrued reversionary bonuses to the date of conversion are typically locked in and remain attached to the paid-up policy.

The reduced sum assured at which a life assurance policy continues in force without further premium payment, after the minimum premium payment period has been satisfied. The policyholder ceases premium payments but retains a smaller policy providing continued life cover (for the reduced sum) until death or maturity. A superior alternative to surrender for policyholders who can no longer afford premiums but wish to retain some life cover.
Formula: Paid-Up Sum Assured = (Premiums Paid ÷ Total Premiums Payable) × Original Sum Assured.

A policy loan is a facility offered by life insurers allowing a policyholder to borrow a sum of money against the security of the policy's surrender value, without surrendering the policy and without going through a conventional credit assessment process. The policy loan is available on endowment and whole life policies that have accumulated a meaningful surrender value — typically after three to five years of premium payment.

The mechanics of a policy loan in Nigerian practice are as follows: the policyholder applies to the insurer for a loan of up to (typically) 80–90% of the current surrender value. The insurer advances the amount, which accrues interest at a rate specified in the policy conditions. The policy remains in force during the loan period; premiums continue to be paid. The loan plus accrued interest is deducted from the benefit payment when a claim arises (on death or maturity). If the loan balance grows to exceed the surrender value — which can occur if premiums lapse and the interest compounds unchecked — the policy is automatically surrendered and the loan is recovered from the surrender proceeds.

blocks.title: Concept in Practice — Policy Loan — A Worked Example

blocks.h: Adaeze holds a 15-year endowment policy with a current surrender value of ₦400,000 and three years remaining to maturity. She requires ₦300,000 urgently for school fees.
She applies for a policy loan of ₦300,000 (75% of surrender value). The insurer advances the amount at 12% per annum, with interest charged monthly. She continues to pay her regular policy premiums.

Outcome on maturity (three years later): Sum assured ₦500,000 + declared reversionary bonuses ₦120,000 + terminal bonus ₦30,000 = Total claim ₦650,000. Less loan outstanding: ₦300,000 + 36 months interest at 12% p.a. = approximately ₦430,000 (if no repayments made). Net payment to Adaeze: ₦650,000 − ₦430,000 = ₦220,000.

Key insight: the policy loan allowed Adaeze to access liquidity without losing her long-term policy. She avoided a surrender that would have yielded only ₦400,000 today, and received a net ₦220,000 at maturity while having also received the ₦300,000 she needed — a total value of ₦520,000 vs. ₦400,000 on immediate surrender. However, if Adaeze's premiums had lapsed and the loan balance had grown unchecked, the policy could have been consumed entirely.

A lien in life assurance is a condition imposed by the insurer — typically at inception for high-risk or non-standard cases — limiting the death benefit payable during an initial period (the 'lien period'). During the lien period, if the life assured dies, the death benefit is reduced to the surrender value (or to the paid-up value, depending on the lien's terms) rather than the full sum assured. After the lien period expires, the full sum assured becomes payable on death.

Liens are used as an alternative to outright declinature for lives that present an elevated but manageable risk — for example, a proposer who has recently recovered from a serious illness but whose health is now stable, or a proposer who has a family history of a serious disease but has not yet manifested symptoms. Instead of refusing cover, the insurer accepts the risk on a limited basis for the first two to three years, giving the life assured the opportunity to demonstrate the stability of their health.

A condition imposed by the insurer on a non-standard life assurance policy, limiting the death benefit payable during an initial lien period (typically 2–5 years) to the surrender value or a reduced sum, rather than the full sum assured. After the lien period expires without a death claim, the policy converts to standard terms and the full sum assured is payable. A lien is a risk management tool used in underwriting as an alternative to outright declinature.
Cf: Rating (a premium loading for elevated risk); Exclusion (an exclusion of a specific cause of death); Declinature (refusal to issue cover).

Life assurance policies fall into one of two broad categories based on whether the policyholder participates in the investment surplus of the insurer's life fund. This structural distinction has profound implications for the premium level, the policy's accumulated value, and the nature of the benefit payable at claim.<sup>[7]</sup>

items.h: A non-participating (without-profit) policy is one in which the benefit is entirely fixed and guaranteed at inception. The policyholder pays a lower premium than under an equivalent participating policy, but the benefit does not grow beyond the guaranteed sum assured. Term assurance is invariably non-participating. Some endowment and whole life policies are issued on non-participating terms.

A participating (with-profit) policy is one in which the policyholder shares in the investment profits generated by the insurer's life fund. The policyholder pays a higher premium than under a non-participating equivalent, but the policy accumulates bonuses that are added to the sum assured, increasing the benefit payable at maturity or on death.

blocks.h: In a participating policy, the insurer invests the premium fund prudently in a portfolio of government bonds, equities, and other admissible assets. Each year, the insurer's actuaries calculate whether the fund has generated a surplus — a profit over and above the amounts needed to meet guaranteed obligations, maintain required reserves, and meet expenses. A portion of this surplus (regulated as at least 90% in many jurisdictions, though Nigerian-specific ratios are set by NAICOM's actuarial guidelines) is allocated to participating policyholders in the form of a bonus declaration.

The 'smoothing' principle is central to the with-profits mechanism: to avoid large year-on-year fluctuations in the bonus rate, insurers do not distribute the full surplus in high-return years but hold back a reserve ('estate') from which bonuses can be sustained in lower-return years. This smoothing creates the relatively stable annual bonus rates that make participating policies commercially attractive as savings vehicles — the policyholder sees consistent annual additions to their policy value rather than the volatility of a directly market-linked fund.

An annual bonus added to the sum assured of a participating life assurance policy, declared by the insurer each year from the surplus of the participating fund. Once declared and vested, it becomes part of the guaranteed benefits of the policy and cannot be withdrawn. It is payable, together with the sum assured, at the time of any claim — on death, maturity, or surrender. Expressed as a percentage of the basic sum assured (simple reversionary bonus) or of the sum assured plus accumulated bonuses to date (compound reversionary bonus).

Example: A ₦1 million sum assured with a simple reversionary bonus of 3.5% per annum would accumulate ₦35,000 of bonus per year. After 10 years: basic sum assured ₦1,000,000 + accrued bonuses ₦350,000 = total benefit ₦1,350,000.

A one-time additional bonus declared by the insurer at the time a participating policy becomes a claim — at maturity, on death, or (sometimes) on surrender. It is entirely discretionary and is not guaranteed at inception. Its purpose is to distribute any remaining accumulated surplus that has not been shared as reversionary bonuses, and to compensate long-term policyholders for the smoothing effect that may have understated their share in high-growth years. The terminal bonus rewards policy continuity: it is typically higher for policies held longer.

Note: Because the terminal bonus is discretionary, it must not be relied upon in financial planning projections. Policy illustrations should present the terminal bonus as 'non-guaranteed' and show a range of scenarios.

A bonus declared by the insurer for the period between the last annual bonus declaration date and the date a claim arises. It is paid to ensure that a policyholder who suffers a loss partway through the year receives a proportionate share of the bonus for the partial year. Interim bonuses are typically calculated as a proportion of the most recently declared reversionary bonus, pro-rated for the number of months elapsed.
Example: If the last reversionary bonus was declared on 1 January and a death occurs on 30 June, six months' interim bonus at a daily or monthly rate is added to the claim.

rows: Annually, based on surplus of the par fund. Calculated as % of basic sum assured only.
Yes — vests immediately on declaration; cannot be reduced
Annually, based on surplus. Calculated as % of (sum assured + accumulated bonuses).
Yes — produces higher absolute amounts than simple bonus over time due to compounding
At claim only (maturity, death, sometimes surrender). Discretionary, based on residual fund surplus.
No — entirely at insurer's discretion; may be zero in bad investment years
Between annual declaration dates; paid when a claim falls in mid-year.
Typically yes, once the claim is accepted — pro-rated from the most recent declared rate

blocks.text: 5.11  NIIRA 2025: Life Policy Disclosure Requirements and Consumer Rights

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 significantly strengthens the consumer disclosure obligations applicable to life insurance policies sold in Nigeria. The Act requires that before a life assurance policy is incepted, the insurer must provide the prospective policyholder with a clear, accessible, and complete disclosure of the key features of the product. This obligation applies to all four classes of life insurance business.<sup>[10]</sup>
The required disclosures include:

items.h: The nature of the product — whether it is term, whole life, endowment, savings-type, or investment-linked — and a clear statement of whether any element of the benefit is non-guaranteed.
The sum assured and, for participating policies, the distinction between the guaranteed sum assured and the non-guaranteed bonus elements.
The premium amount, payment mode, and total premium payable over the policy term.
The key exclusions — events for which no benefit is payable — in plain and accessible language, not buried in technical conditions.
The claims procedure: how to notify a claim, what documentation is required, and the 60-day settlement timeline.
The surrender value at indicative intervals (typically years 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, and at maturity), disclosed on a basis approved by NAICOM.
The policy's cooling-off right — the right to cancel within the prescribed period and receive a refund.

blocks.h: For participating policies, the insurer must provide a benefit illustration showing the policy's projected maturity benefit under two scenarios: one using a moderate assumed bonus rate and one using a lower (stressed) assumed rate. Both scenarios must be presented as projections, not guarantees. The illustration must clearly identify which elements are guaranteed (the basic sum assured) and which are not (bonus projections).

NAICOM's market conduct guidelines specifically prohibit the practice of illustrating maturity benefits using historically high bonus rates as though those rates will persist for the full policy term. This practice — widespread in the market before NIIRA 2025 — created systematically unrealistic expectations among policyholders, contributing to disappointment and lapse when actual bonuses fell below the illustrated figures.

blocks.title: Regulatory Spotlight — NIIRA 2025 — Consumer Rights Summary for Life Policyholders

blocks.h: A life insurance policyholder in Nigeria benefits from the following consumer rights under NIIRA 2025:

items.h: Right to a Policy Document: The insurer must provide a complete policy document at inception, in plain and accessible language, covering all benefits, exclusions, conditions, and key terms.
Right to a Key Features Document: A summary of the main benefits, exclusions, premium obligations, and claims procedure in a simplified format suitable for a retail policyholder.

Cooling-Off Right: The right to cancel the policy and receive a full premium refund within the prescribed period (15–30 days from inception or policy delivery, as specified by NAICOM) less any pro-rata cost of cover already consumed.
Right to Accurate Surrender Value Quotations: On request, the insurer must provide a current, accurate surrender value quotation reflecting both the GSV and SSV.
Right to Nomination: The right to nominate a beneficiary and to change the nomination at any time during the policy term, with the insurer obligated to maintain current nominee records.
Right to Claims Settlement within 60 Days: Valid claims must be settled within 60 days of notification; delayed settlement attracts compound interest penalties.
Right to NAICOM Redress: Any unresolved complaint may be referred to NAICOM's Consumer Complaints Bureau without charge.

blocks.h: These rights represent a material improvement in the consumer protection framework for life insurance in Nigeria. The practitioner's obligation is not merely to know these rights but to actively inform clients of them at the point of sale — this is both an ethical obligation under the CIIN Code of Ethics and a regulatory obligation under NIIRA 2025.<sup>[10]</sup>
This chapter has built the terminological and conceptual vocabulary for the study of life assurance products in Nigeria. The following are the chapter's essential propositions.

items.h: 'Life assurance' traditionally refers to cover against a certain event (death) and 'life insurance' to cover against a contingent event. In practice and in NIIRA 2025, both terms are used, with 'life insurance' as the statutory umbrella. The distinction remains analytically important for pricing, actuarial treatment, and regulatory classification.

NIIRA 2025 classifies life insurance business into four statutory classes: (1) individual life assurance; (2) group life assurance; (3) annuity; and (4) health insurance. Each class requires specific regulatory authorisation; a licence for one class does not authorise another.

Five roles are recognised in life assurance: the proposer (who applies and bears disclosure duty); the policyholder (who holds contractual rights); the life assured (on whose life the risk is written); the beneficiary/nominee (who receives proceeds); and the annuitant (on whose survival an annuity income depends).

The sum assured is the guaranteed payment on the specified event — not a cap on indemnity, but a contractual commitment. The premium is the consideration; the policy term is the period of cover. Maturity is the successful endpoint for savings-type policies.

Premiums may be paid in single, annual, semi-annual, quarterly, or monthly modes. The grace period (15–30 days) maintains cover during temporary non-payment. Lapse occurs when the premium is not paid within the grace period. A lapsed policy may be revived within the revival window on production of medical evidence and payment of arrears with interest.

Benefits include the death benefit (payable on death in force), survival benefits (periodic payments in money-back policies), and the maturity benefit (payable on surviving to the end of a fixed-term policy). The surrender value and paid-up value protect the policyholder's accumulated interest on early exit or cessation of premiums.

A policy loan allows the policyholder to borrow against the surrender value without surrendering the policy. A lien limits the death benefit during an initial period as a risk management tool for substandard lives.

Participating (with-profit) policies share the insurer's investment surplus with policyholders through reversionary bonuses (annual, guaranteed once declared), terminal bonuses (at claim, discretionary), and interim bonuses (for mid-year claims). Non-participating policies provide a guaranteed fixed benefit at a lower premium.

NIIRA 2025 requires comprehensive disclosure at point of sale: guaranteed vs non-guaranteed benefits, accurate surrender value quotations, premium totals, key exclusions, and the cooling-off right. Bonus projections for participating policies must present two scenarios and clearly distinguish guaranteed from projected elements.

blocks.h: A long-term insurance contract under which the insurer undertakes to pay a specified sum on the death of the life assured or on another specified life event. 'Assurance' reflects the certainty of the triggering event (death); 'insurance' is used when the event is contingent. The terms are used interchangeably in Nigerian commercial practice.
The person who applies for the insurance by completing the proposal form. Bears the duty of utmost good faith. Becomes the policyholder on acceptance.
The person who holds the insurance policy and owns its contractual rights — the right to alter, surrender, assign, nominate beneficiaries, and make a claim.
The person on whose life the policy is written. Not necessarily the same as the policyholder. The death, survival, or health event of the life assured triggers the benefit payment.

The person designated to receive the policy proceeds on the specified event. A nominee under a nomination clause receives proceeds as the policyholder's representative; an assignee or trust beneficiary receives proceeds outside the estate.
The person on whose life an annuity contract is written. The annuity income is payable for as long as the annuitant lives.
The pre-agreed contractual payment under a life assurance policy on the occurrence of the specified event. Not an indemnity for financial loss — a guaranteed benefit.
Synonymous with the basic sum assured — the initial guaranteed benefit before bonus additions.

The monetary consideration paid by the policyholder to the insurer in exchange for the assumption of risk. May be paid as a single premium or regular premiums (annual, semi-annual, quarterly, or monthly).
The additional charge applied to premiums paid more frequently than annually, compensating the insurer for the time value of the premium instalments.
The period during which the insurance cover is in force.
The date on which a fixed-term life assurance policy expires and the maturity benefit becomes payable to the surviving policyholder.
The period (typically 15–30 days) after a premium due date during which the policy remains in force despite non-payment. Death during the grace period is covered, less any unpaid premium.
The termination of a life assurance policy due to non-payment of premiums beyond the grace period. A lapsed policy provides no cover.
The reduced sum assured at which a policy continues without further premium payment. Calculated as the proportion of premiums actually paid over total premiums due.

The amount payable by the insurer to a policyholder who voluntarily terminates the policy before maturity. Calculated as the higher of the Guaranteed Surrender Value (GSV) or the Special Surrender Value (SSV).
A loan advanced by the insurer against the security of the policy's surrender value, without surrendering the policy. The loan balance plus interest is deducted from the claim payment.
An underwriting condition limiting the death benefit during an initial period for a substandard-risk life. After the lien period, the full sum assured is payable.

A life assurance policy under which the policyholder shares in the investment surplus of the insurer's participating fund through bonus declarations. Generally carries a higher premium than a non-participating equivalent.
A life assurance policy with a fixed, guaranteed benefit and no share in investment surplus. Lower premium; no bonus additions.
An annual bonus declared from the surplus of a participating fund and added to the sum assured. Guaranteed once declared; payable at the time of any valid claim.
A discretionary one-time bonus declared at the time a participating policy becomes a claim. Not guaranteed; rewards long-term policy holding.
A bonus covering the period from the last annual declaration to a mid-year claim date. Pro-rated from the most recently declared reversionary bonus rate.
